Preface
For an all around development of a child it is very important
the understand child psychology. All modern psychologists
hold that every individual should have, at least, little acquaintance
with child Psychology as it helps in solving children's problem
all the better.
This book discusses all the aspects that influence the growth
and development of children. Child Psychology has added a
new dimension to the vast knowledge of the subject. It
introduces various stages of child development right from the
conception tothe adolescence. The book is divided in two
parts the first part deals with the psychological part and the
part deals with the developmental part.
The main objective for writing this book is to analyses the
impacts of environment and heredity on child's development
with psychology. Role of family is very important in child
development because the environmental a child gets at home
affects the child psychology a lot. The stages of growth such
as infancy, childhood and adolescence, laying emphasis on
social and psychological development of the child. Then the
book discusses problems of genetic psychology in the child.
Many problems are due to genetic transfer.
Preface
This book is beneficial for students, teachers, researchers,
psychologists and for general readers.

the Child
The psychological development that starts at birth and terminates
in adulthood is comparable to organic growth. Like the latter, it
consists essentially of activity directed toward equilibrium.Just as
the body evolves toward a relatively stable level characterised by
the completion of the growth process and by organ maturity, so
mental life can be conceived as evolving toward a final form of
equilibrium represented by the adult mind. In a sense, development
is a progressive equilibration from a lesser to a higher state of

TheNeonate and the Infant
The periodthat extends from birth to the acquisition of language
is marked by an extraordinary development of the mind. Its
importance is sometimes underestimated because it is not
accompanied by words that permit a step-by-step pursuit of the
progress of intelligence and the emotions, as is the case later on.
Thisearly mental development nonetheless determines the entire
course ot psychological evolution. In fact, it is no less than a
Conquest by perception and movement of the entire practical
universe thatsurrounds the smallchild,At eighteen monthsto two
years this `sensorimotor assimilation' of the immediate external
world effectsa miniature Copernican revolution. Atthestarting
Mental Development of the Child

point of this development the neonate grasps everything to
himself-or, in more precise terms,to his own body--whereas at
the termination of this period, i.e.,when language and thought
begin, he is for all practical purposes but one elemernt or entity
amongothers in a universe that he has gradually constructed himself,
and which hereafter he will experience as external to himself.
Step by step, we shall describe the stages of this Copernican
revolution in its two-fold aspect of intelligence and nascent affective
life.With respect to the development of intelligence, we have
already cited three stages between birth and the end of the first
period: the reflex stage, the stage of the organisation of percepts
and habits, and the stage of sensorimotor intelligence itself.
At birth, mental life is limited to the exercise of reflex
apparatuses, i.e., of hereditarily determined sensory and motor
coordinations that correspond to instinctual needs, such as nutrition.
Totheextent that these reflexes bear on the behaviour that will play
arole in subsequent psychological development, they have none of
the mechanical passivity that might be attributed tothem.On the
contrary, fromthevery outset, they manifest genuine activity, which
is the best evidence for the existence of precocious sensorimotor
assimilation. The sucking reflexes, for example, become refined, and
the neonate sucks better after one or two weeks than during the
first days. Ata somewhat later age, these reflexes lead to practical
discriminations and recognitions that are easily observed. Still later,
and most important, these reflexes give rise to a kind of
generalisation ofactivity. The infant is not content to suck onlywhen
;he also sucks at random. He sucks his fingers when he

degree that his initial behaviour can be described by saying that for
him the world is essentially a thing to be sucked. In short order,
this same universe will also become a thing to be looked at, to listen
to, and as soon as his own movements allow, to shake.

Let us see how these acts of intelligence are constructed. Two
kinds of factors are involved. First of all, early behaviour becomes
increasingly elaborated and differentiated tothe point where the
infant acquires sufficient behavioural facility for him to notice the
results of his actions. In these 'circular reactions' the baby is not
content merely to reproduce movements and gestures that have led
to an interesting effect. He varies them intentionally in order to study
the results of these variations and thus gives himself over to true
explorations or to 'experiments in order to see'. This is exemplified
by the behaviour of the twelve-month-old child who throws
objects on the ground in one direction or another in order to see
how and where they fall.
Secondly, the 'action schemata' constructed at the previous stage
and multiplied through new experimental behaviours become
capable of coordinating with one another through a process of
reciprocal assimilation. This proces is analogous to what will occur
later in the ideas or conceptsof thought itself. In effect, an action
that can be repeated and generalised to a new situation might be
thought of as a kind of sensorimotor concept. For example, a baby
presented with a new object successively incorporates it into each
of his'actionschemata' (shaking it, stroking it, balancing it, etc.) as
though he could come to know the object by perceiving how it
is used. (At five or six years children still define concepts by starting
with the words,It is for': a table is for writing on', etc.) The
sensorimotor assimilation at this stage is comparable to what will

Later on he will look for the hidden object but without noticing

It is only toward the end of the first year that objects are sought
out when they leave the perceptual field; this is a criterion for the
beginning of the externalisation of the material world. In short, the
initial absence of substantive objects, followed by the construction
of solid and permanent objects, is the first example of the transition
from primitive, total egocentricity to the final elaboration of an
external universe.
The evolution of practical space is entirely at one with the
construction of objects. At the outset there are as many spaces
uncoordinated among themselves as sensory fields (oral spaces,
visual spaces, tactile spaces, etc.), and each one of them is centred
on the child's own movements and activity. Visual space, 1n
particular, does not have the same depth at the outset that it will
have later on. By the end of the second year, however, a sense of
general space has been acquired which includes all the other
particular spaces and which is characterised by relationships among
objects and between objects and the child's own body. The
elaboration of space is essentially derived from the coordination
of movements so that there is adirect relationship between the
development of a sense of space and of sensorimotor intelligence.

This being so, it is clear that during the initial stage of reflex
techniques there are correspondingelementary instinctive strivings
linked with nutrition as well as the kind of affective reflexes that
constitute the primary emotions. Recently the relationship between
the emotions and the physiological system of attitudes and postures
has been shown. The first fears, for example, can be related to losses
of equilibrium or to sudden contrasts between a fortuitous event
and a preceding attitude
At the second stage (percepts and habits), as well as at the
beginnings ofsensorimotor intelligence, there is a corresponding
series of elementary emotions or affective percepts linked to the
modalities of activity itself: the agreeable or the disagreeable,
pleasure and pain, etc., as well as the first realisations of success
and failure. To the extent that these affective statesdepend on action
per seandnot as yet on awareness of relationships with other people,
this level of affectivity attests to a kind of general egocentricity and
gives the impression, if one mistakenly attributes a sense of self
to the baby, of a kind of love of self and of one's own activity.
Itistrue that the infant begins by being mainly interested in his own
body, in its movements and in the results ofhis actions. Psychoanalysis
has called this elementary stage of affectivity 'narcissism', but it is
important to understand that it is a narcissism without Narcissus,
i.e., without any sense of personal awareness as such.
With the development of intelligence, however, and with the
ensuing elaboration of an external universe and especially with the
construction of the schema ofthe 'object', a third level of affectivity
appears. It is epitomised, in the language of psychoanalysis, by the
object choice, ie, by the objectivation ofthe emotions and by their
projection onto activities other than those of the self alone. Let us
note, first of all, that with the progress of intelligent behaviour the
emotions linked to activity become differentiated and multiplied:
joy and sadness linked to success and failure of intentional acts,
effort linked to interest, or fatigue to disinterest, etc. These affective
states, like those associated with perception, stay linked for a long
time to the isolated actions ofthe subject without precise delimitation
between what is specifice to him and what is attributable to the

Early Childhood from Two to Seven Years
With the appearance oflanguage, behaviour is profoundly modified

This has three consequences essential to mental development: (1)

words,i.e., the appearance of thought itself, supported by internal

Childhood from Seven to Twelve Years
The age of seven years, which coincides with the real start of formal
education,marks a decisive turning point in mental development.
In each of the complex areas of psychological life, whether it be
intelligence, affectivity, social relations, or individual activity, ne
forms of organisation appear. These new forms of organisation
assure the completion and more stabilised equilibrium of
constructions already outlined inthe precedingperiod and inaugurate
an uninterrupted series of new constructions.
Through this labyrinth we shall follow the same routes as in
the pervious section. We shall start with global action-both social
and individual--and first analyse the intellectual and then the
affective aspects of development during this period.

omnipotence ofreflection, as though the world should submit itself

metaphysical age par excellence; the self is strong enough to
reconstruct the universe and big enough to incorporate it.
Then, just as the sensorimotor egocentricity ofearly childhood

formal thought and reality is affected. Equilibrium is attained when
the adolescent understands that the proper function of reflection
is not to contradict but to predict and interpret experience. This
formal equilibrium surpasses by far the equilibrium of concrete
thought because it not only encompasses the real world but also
the undefined constructions of rational deduction and inner life.

Models of Equilibrium

thermodynamics, in physical chemistry, in biology, in econometrics,
etc., and all kinds of terms have been used with respect to them.

Conclusion
Generally speaking, the equilibrium of cognitive structures can be
conceived as a compensation for external intrusion by means of
the activities of the subject, which are responses to these intrusions.
The latter may be presented in two different ways.
In the case of the lower, unstable (sensorimotor and perceptual)
forms of equilibrium, the intrusion consists of real and actual
modifications of the environment, to which the compensatory
activities of the subject respond as best they can without a
permanent operational system. These are the forms of equilibrium
described above aproposof the law of the temporal maximum
ofillusions.
In the case of the higher or operational structures, on the other
hand, the intrusion to which the subject responds may consist of
virtual modifications; ie, in optimum cases they can be imagined
and anticipated by the subject in the form of the direct operations
of a system (operations expressing transformations in some initial
sense). In this case, the compensatory activities will also consist of
Imagining and anticipating the transformations but in an inverse
sense (reciprocal or inverse operations of a system of reversble
operations).
In short, the compensations start by being effectuated by
degrees but can end by consisting of pure representations of the
transformations with the intrusions, like the compensations, being
reduced to certain operations of the system. Between these two
extremes there are, of course, all kinds of intervening steps, Such

virtual transformations correspond to the subject's real operations.
This is why the concept of equilibrium is explicative in psychology.

A fundamental factor must be taken into account. This is that
objects are constantly changed through action and that these
transformations constitute new sources of knowledge. One ofKarl

by acting on them and by producing some transformation in them.
For example the logical operations of classifying or seriating consist
of 'producing' collections or a certain order of succession by means
of the properties of the objects employed.

A fourth factor nust be mentioned which is too often
forgotten but whoseimportance will undoubtedly be shown
increasingly in future research. This is the factor ofequilibrium
linked toprobabilistic considerations. First of all, it is apparent that
cach of the preceding three factors is subject to laws of equilibrium
and that their interaction involves a form of equilibration. The
coordination of the actions of an individual subject is manifested
through momentary disequilibria (corresponding to needs
problems) and through re-cquilibration (correspondingto satisfactions
or solutions). It goes without saying that the social coordination of
actions involves both disequilibria and forms of equilibrium and
that the interactions among the personal (neurological, etc.) factors
and the social factors ofaction stem from acontinual equilibration.
But the notion of equilibrium has a much more precise meaning
in the psychology of logical operations than it does in other fields.
We have seen that an operation is essentially a reversible action, since
for any given operation (such as +A or +1) there is always its
corresponding inverse (-A or -1). It is this reversibility which
enables the child to understand the conservation of a quantity or
of a set when its spatial disposition is altered, since when the
modification is seen as reversible, it follows that the quantity in
question remains invariant. Reversibility develops progressively in
the course of the child's mental evolution, The child at the
sensorimnotor level is aware only of a practical reversibility in
proximal space (the 'group of displacements' built up during the
second year of life) and the preoperational representations only
present a semireversibility on the plane of thought linked to
approximate regulations or compensations (correctionof a gross
error, etc.). Theconcrete operations comprise two parallel forms
of reversibility, inversion or negation in the operations of classes
and reciprocity in the operations of relations. Finally, at the level
of the formal operations, the INRCgroup fuses these two torms
of reversibility into a single system through the establishment o
inversions and reciprocities. This growing reversibilty aSs

According to the ethologists, cach species of animal is born with

distress. But ifthe moving object that the ducklingsees during the
critical period for imprinting is something else, such as a human

instead of the mother duck.

Jean Piaget's Influential Theory

Iean Piaget was the most influential developmental psychologist of
the twentieth century. Largely as a result of his theoretical and
empirical work, cognition has heldcentre stagein child development
wRSearch since 1960. As we shall see, his theory of cognitive growth
and change is original, conmprehensive, integrative and elegant.
Piaget died in 1980 at the age of 84. Throughout his long life,
he made meticulous observations and records of infants' and
children's spontaneous activities, devised many ingenious 'tests' of
cognitive abilities, and presented problems to thousands of children
and adolescents. He was a prolific writer, publishing more than 30
books and 200 articles.
Piaget's ideas have been the source of an untold number of
research studies, but they have also generated considerable
controversy. As we shall see, many experts have pointed out
weaknesses in Piaget's research and questioned his conclusions. But
the criticisms ofPiaget have been productive; "much of our most
exciting information about intellectual development comes from
experimenters whose starting point was either a doubt about one
or another ofPiaget's conclusions or a desire to defend him against
his critics".
Our discussion begins with the fundamental concepts of
Piaget's theory. Bear in mind that the theory deals exclusively with
cognitive development, beginning with the primitive reflexes and
motor coordinations of infancy and extending to the thinking and
problem solving of adolescents and adults. Scientific and
mathematical abilities are stressed-abstract and logical reasoning,
generationof hypotheses, and organisingmental activities into more
CompleX structures. Piaget was not concerned with motives,
emotions, personality characteristics, or social behaviour, although
some psychologists have found his concepts useful in understanding
these issues.
In Piaget's theory, knowledge is assumed to have a specific goal
Opurpose: to aid the person in adapting to the environment. The

Piaget's central thesis is that the individual is active, curious. and

The major mechanisms that allow children to progress from one
stage of cognitive functioning to the next are called by Piaget
assimilation, accommodation, and equilibration. Assimilation reters
to the individual's effortsto dealwith the environment by making
it fit into the organism'sown existing structures--by incorporatns

Piaget suggested that there is a complementary process,
accommodation, which is "the individual'stendency to change in
response to environmental demands", that is, to modify actions and
ideas (schemes) to fit new situations, objects, or information. The
5-year-old girl realises that she needs a new category for this new
object, a helicopter, which cannot be assimilated to her concept of
bird. If shequestions her parents, they will supply anew word and
explain the differences between birds and helicopters, permiting
the child to create the new category.
As a result of this new knowledge, the child is temporarily in
state that Piaget calls equilibrium, or cognitive harmony. Piaget
assumes that all organisms strive for balance in their interactions with
their environment. When an individual's equilibrium is disturbed
tor example, when something new and interesting is encountered
the processes of assimilation and accommodation function to re
establish it. (The process of establishing equilibrium is known as
equilibration). The child first attempts to understand a new experience
by using old ideas and solutions (assimilation); when these do not
work, the child is forced to change her structure or understanding
of the world (accommodation).

Cognitive Development in Child

Thus, Piaget insists that some cognitive ideas, operations, and
structures are universal, not because they are inherited but because
all children's ordinary experiences in the world of objects and
people force them to comne to the same conclusions and acquire
the same cognitive structures. Piaget believes that all children
eventually learn to group less abstract categories like dog into more
abstract categories like pets or animals. All children come to realise
that all categories can be taken apart into at least two smaller sets;
the category animals can be separated into two smaller classes: dogs
and all the animals that are not dogs. Similarly, all children come
to realise that events can be ordered by their magnitude from the
smallest to the largest or the lightest to the heaviest. These rules as
well as a great many others develop, Piaget claims, because of the
everyday interactions that children have with objects and people,
interactions that through the process of accommodation and
equilibrium lead to new mnental structure.

Problems of Socio-Economic Change
It will be appreciated that social and economic change throws up
its own problems for a dynamic society. It does not bring with it
automatic solutions. Society or some of its members like social
workers and thinkers have to be vigilant to study the effects and
consequences of socio-economic transformation and recommend
suitable remedial and preventive measures to tackle the rising social
ills and problems. Some of the needs of society, particularly in
rapidly urbanising populations, are by now well known. They are
adequate housing, health services, education, employment, proper
use of leisure and the sense of belonging to the community.
These services have to be provided for all age-groups, and
particularly for children, for the simple reason that they form the
largest and most vulnerable section of society,they will make its
future citizens and they will be part of it for the longest span of
time. Ifthe preventive and constructive services are not provided,

weaken the comnunity and cost society heavily in money and
wasted human lives.

Early Efforts
The Society for the Protection of Childrenin Western India has
remained a pioneer organisation in the field of Prevention and
Treatment ofJuvenileDelinquency in India. Thanksto the arduous
efforts ofeminent socialthinkers like Sir Rustom Masaniand Sir
JohnWardlawMilne, the founders ofthis society, and their band
of zealous colleagues, it was during the World War I that public
attention was focused on the problems of waifs and strays in
Mumbai. It was possible to organise and experimental shelter for
such children in Mumbai as early as 1916, preparatory to the
establishment ofthe Society in January 1917.
Existing Welfare Services
The Mumbai Children Act was passed in 1924 but actuallyit was
made operative in 1927. The new Act made new demands tor
strengthening government in putting the provisions of the Act into
operation. The Children's Aid Society was formed and, under the
able guidance of Miss M.K. Davis, M.B.E., a Remand Home was
started in the old Jail building at Umarkhadi. Since then wellare
services for children in need have shown a rising curve in the

replaced bythepresent legislation, viz. The MumbaiChildren Act,
1948. Special facilities for temporary detention of children on
remand in the form of Remand Homes are now made available
in 23 districts of the State of Mumbai as it is constituted to-day.
Over and above the 14 Government Certified Schools, a large
number of voluntary organisations working in the field of
Prevention and Treatment of Juvenile Delinquency have been
recognised as voluntary Certified Schools or Fit Person Institutions
throughout the State of Mumbai. The tabulated statement at the
end of this book shows at a glance how expensive is the work
of social service for children in need.
It has been my good fortune to have been associated with the
Society for the Protection of Children in Western India for the last
21 years in various capacities: I began my career as Superintendent
in the B.J. Home for Children, Matunga, conducted by the Society.

My next assignment was in the Government set-up at the Yeravda
Industrial School, Poona, which is the largest State institution, a
Certified School meant for the hardened type of delinquent boys
under the Mumbai Children Act. I was also Inspector of Certified
Schools for a short time and later on Chief Inspector of Certified
Schools under the Mumbai Children Act. I deem it a privilege that
I havenow an opportunity to look back on the last 30 years and
make a few broad observations on the problem of delinquency
in the State of Mumbai.
Classification of Homes
The practice today is that administrative authorities classify the
institutions and send children committed by theJuvenile Courts to
them,taking into account the plan of social rehabilitation of the
individualchild. The B.J. Home for Children is one of the foremost
institutions where children needing protection, showing signs of
predelinquent behaviour and manifesting other behaviour disorders
which have not come to the notice of Law have been cared for.
On the other hand, the B.J. Home for Children has always been
an institution where children of the preadolescent age group who

can be educated have been sent, This Homealso affords facilities
tokeep brothers and sisters together as it has a Girls' Home and
a Boys' Home in the same premises.Asstatedabove, the Yeravda
Industrial Schoolhas been used mostly for boyswith a known
delinquency history. The behaviour problems manifest among the
chidlren at the Yeravda Industrial School, Poone, were nore
marked and deep-rooted and therefore the physical set-up of the
institution issuch as gives more attention to security measures.
Problems Basically the Same
On the whole, however, I feel that the problems ofchildren in need
are basically the same. In a large number of cases the children have
been found to be parentless. Unwanted in their own family set-up,
the maiorityof them have had a broken family history. They have
taken to a street lifewith its consequent results of association with
bad characters, gangs and adult criminals.
As regards girls, the problems have been somewhat different.
Although it is true that girls are more protected from outside
harmful influences, the fact remains that in the lower strata of
society they are not free from dangers. Many ofthe girls have been
victims of kidnappers who wanted them to lead a life of
immorality. At times girls who have no adequate superivision in their
homes have been decoyed by bad characters or taken advantage
of by irresponsible persons in the neighbourhood. Often it was
found that mothers in broken families, even amongthe sophisticated
classes, have taken to rather dubious, professions, which necessitated
keeping them in institutions to protect them from going astray.
There were instances in which the girls had to be kept in the
institutions because the mothers had remarried and the new families
did not offer the needed protection tothem.
The problems of rehabilitation also differed considerably. The
boys who had been in institutions were generally trained in certaun
crafts and employment had to be found for them, while the main
avenue rehabilitation in respect of girls was marriage.
Looking to individual cases of children, I am inclined to teel
that the line of demarcation between theso-called delinquent cases
DelinquentChild
onthe one hhand andthe protection cases onthe other is verythin.
In fact, one cannot drawsuch a distinctionexcept forconvenience.
Ir often happens that a so-called hardened and delinquent boy, when
heis sent to an institution meant for this type of children, betrays
no symptom of delinquency, establishing that it was only in a fit
of emotion that he committed his first offence which caused him
to be treated under the Children Act. On the other hand. there have
been cases of children who, though they are called protective cases,
have had a long history of delinquent behaviour in the family set
n as well as in the neighbourhood, but some-sow managed to
escape the notice of the law.
It follows therefore that the organisations of treatment facilities
must be adapted to each individual child rather than laid down on
a mass Scale.
Too Much of Institutional Treatment

It is also curious that methods of treatment other than the
institutional do not receive sufficient attention. The method of
keeping a child on probation is, for instance, not used adequately.

Institutional Improvements Needed
As regards institutional treatment, there is a tendency among the
promoters of institutions to have large units. Many a time a
comparison is drawn between such institutions and the laroe
Rishikuls' of ancient India. Needless to say, such comparisons are
faulty. It has been proved by experience that the success of
treatment and rehabilitation depends on the rapport which the
institutional personnel can establish with the individualchild.
Large institutions with inadequate staff do not at all offer any
promise of therapeutic contact. In fact, it is not possible for the
Superintendents to know their charge properly. The child comes
out of the institution with the feeling that he or she is more
unwanted now than when he or she was admitted into it!
Though concentrated efforts are made to improve occupational
training and recreational facilities in institutions, the gap between
existing facilities and actual needs of a therapeutic programme is
still wide.
Training of the staff has always been an improvement ned

Now it is admitted on all handsthat institution personnel must not
only possess proper personality, experience and temperament, but

After-care

urgent problem has been touched. After-care facilities continue to
the inadequate and the result of this has not been salutary.The
standard ofliving in the institutions, on the one hand, and íin the

This lacuna has been receiving the attention ofthe country's

As the country advances, emerging from theold rural culture

The Role of the Police
The role of the police depends not on its size, but onthe quality
of the persons comprising it. The effectiveness of delinquency
control is predicated on theliaisoning betweenthe work of the
Control and Prevention of Delinquency

effective court system and an adequate juvenile law. The activities
ofunscrupulous adults who exploit juveniles for their own means
must be curbed. Areas or places of social vice and cheap
commercialised recreation which exercise baneful influence on the
iuvenile's mind must be watched. These unhealthy elements go
counter to or negate the good influence which education, religion,
and the familyculture induces in the growing mind of the juvenile.
The first thing necessary which the school, the family and the
community should do is to wean away the juvenile from all
unhealthy influences and contacts.
There should be no differential norms of conduct and
behaviour for the juvenile and the adult. What is good for the
juvenile is good for the adult, and vice versa. Both the juvenile and
the adult must owe allegiance to a common moral social and ethical
code ofstandards and behaviour. The control over sharp practices
has to be exercised through adequate enforcement of law, Character
building through informal education in schools and through
recreation clubs on the play-ground should be made a part and
parcelof the culturalcomponent ofthe juvenle's personality. Moral
fibre must be strengthened at all stages of his development. Inspite
ofall these measures, certain deviation or unadjustment may result
in delinquency in certain cases especially in urban areas. To offset
or counteract this deviation in an urban child, it would be necessary
to provide facilities for referral topsychiatric or behaviour clinic.

found in difficulty. After the juvenile has been picked up by the
police, the officer concerned should interview him with understanding
and sympathy. He should find out if the juvenile has his parents
